answer.sourceLine: Confirmed against the primary text. The sentence appears in Maslow’s paper “A Theory of Human Motivation” ↗, Psychological Review 50, no. 4 (1943), on p. 382 — in the paragraph that first defines self-actualization. The wording is exact: no paraphrase, no tidying up.

source.excerpt: Even if all these needs are satisfied, we may still often (if not always) expect that a new discontent and restlessness will soon develop, unless the individual is doing what he is fitted for. A musician must make music, an artist must paint, a poet must write, if he is to be ultimately happy. What a man can be, he must be. This need we may call self-actualization.
trail: The complete 1943 paper is transcribed at Classics in the History of Psychology ↗, Christopher D. Green’s archive at York University. Searching the text returns the sentence once, inside the section headed “The need for self-actualization,” between the [p. 382] and [p. 383] markers.

Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ carries the same sentence and cites Psychological Review vol. 50, no. 4 (1943), p. 382, adding that it also appears in Motivation and Personality (1954), p. 93. The page has no Misattributed or Disputed section for Maslow.

Wikipedia’s hierarchy of needs article ↗ quotes the line but cites Maslow 1954, p. 91 — the book, not the paper. That mismatch between p. 91, p. 93 and the 1943 original is the main thing this page fixes.
Quote Investigator ↗ returns no article for this quotation, which is what you would expect: it is not a contested line, only a carelessly cited one.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the full text of the 1943 article; the passage falls between the transcription’s [p. 382] and [p. 383] page markers. Note the lead-in clause: the article reads “ultimately happy,” where the widely reprinted form reads “ultimately at peace with himself.”

author.name: Abraham Maslow
author.heading: About Abraham Maslow
author.metaLine: 1908–1970 · American psychologist, Brooklyn College and Brandeis University
author.bio: Abraham Maslow (1908–1970) was an American psychologist who taught at Brooklyn College from 1937 to 1951 and at Brandeis University from 1951 to 1969. His 1943 Psychological Review paper “A Theory of Human Motivation” laid out the ladder of needs — physiological, safety, love, esteem — that tops out in self-actualization, the step this one sentence exists to define. He expanded the argument into Motivation and Personality (Harper, 1954), the book most people reach for when they quote him.

misattribution.heading: What usually goes wrong
misattribution.intro: The name on this quote is right. What gets mangled is the source, the credit for the term, and the sentence immediately before it.

items.why: Wikipedia’s hierarchy of needs article ↗ quotes the line and cites “Maslow 1954, p. 91”; Wikiquote cites p. 93 of the same book. Both point at the reprint. The sentence was already in print in 1943, in Psychological Review.

In the same paragraph Maslow writes that “self-actualization” was “first coined by Kurt Goldstein,” and that he is using it “in a much more specific and limited fashion” — his words, on p. 382 ↗. Goldstein supplied the label. The sentence is Maslow’s.

The 1943 article reads “if he is to be ultimately happy.” The form that circulates most widely — and that Wikiquote records ↗ — is “ultimately at peace with himself.” If you quote the fuller passage, the two forms are not interchangeable. The target sentence itself is identical in both.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is Maslow’s own, and it first reached print in 1943, in Psychological Review 50, no. 4, p. 382 ↗ — eleven years before the 1954 book almost everyone cites instead.

context.heading: Why this sentence mattered
lead: Maslow’s 1943 paper is famous for its staircase — physiological needs, then safety, then love, then esteem. The trouble with a staircase is that it has to end somewhere, and Maslow needed a top step that wasn’t just “more esteem.” This sentence is that top step. Everything below it is a deficit you are trying to close; this one is a capacity you are trying to spend.

The setup does the work: “A musician must make music, an artist must paint, a poet must write.” Then the compression — what a man can be, he must be — and immediately the label: “This need we may call self-actualization.” Maslow is careful in the very next line to hand the term to Kurt Goldstein ↗, saying he is using it “in a much more specific and limited fashion.” The borrowed word, the original sentence.
detailsBody: The paragraph opens on a warning rather than a promise: “Even if all these needs are satisfied, we may still often (if not always) expect that a new discontent and restlessness will soon develop, unless the individual is doing what he is fitted for.” Read whole, the line is less a motivational slogan than a diagnosis of why satisfied people are still restless.

Maslow immediately hedges the scope, too: “The specific form that these needs will take will of course vary greatly from person to person.” The must is not a command about ambition — it is a claim that the shape of the need is individual and non-negotiable.
context.pull: Everything lower on the ladder is a hole you are filling. This is the one rung that is about spending what you have.

sourcesVerified.claim: The full text of Maslow's 1943 Psychological Review paper contains the exact sentence "What a man can be, he must be." on p. 382, preceded by "A musician must make music, an artist must paint, a poet must write, if he is to be ultimately happy." and followed by "This need we may call self-actualization."
In the same paragraph Maslow writes that the term self-actualization was "first coined by Kurt Goldstein" and is used in his paper "in a much more specific and limited fashion."

The transcription's header states: A. H. Maslow (1943), "A Theory of Human Motivation," originally published in Psychological Review, 50, 370-396; hosted by Classics in the History of Psychology, developed by Christopher D. Green, York University.

Wikiquote's sourced section for Abraham Maslow carries the line "What a man can be, he must be" citing "A Theory of Human Motivation" in Psychological Review, vol. 50, no. 4 (1943), p. 382, and notes it also appears in Motivation and Personality (1954), p. 93; the wording it gives for the lead-in is "if he is to be ultimately at peace with himself." The page has no Misattributed or Disputed section.

Wikipedia's Maslow's hierarchy of needs article quotes "What a man can be, he must be." and cites it to Maslow 1954, p. 91, and states the hierarchy was introduced in the 1943 paper "A Theory of Human Motivation" in Psychological Review.

Abraham Maslow lived 1 April 1908 to 8 June 1970, was an American psychologist, taught at Brooklyn College 1937-1951 and Brandeis University 1951-1969; "A Theory of Human Motivation" appeared in Psychological Review, 1943, vol. 50, issue 4, pp. 370-396, and Motivation and Personality was first published in 1954.
Psychological Review was founded in 1894 and is published/owned by the American Psychological Association.
The Internet Archive catalogues Maslow's Motivation and Personality, published by Harper, New York, 1954, as an access-restricted lending-only scan.
